sb_prompt: DISCUSS CRIME IN AMERICAN CITIES TODAY.  WHAT ARE YOUR CONCERNS AND THE CONCERNS OF THE OTHER CALLER?  WHAT STEPS CAN BE TAKEN TO REDUCE CRIME?
turns: Yeah, look, I was talking to my cousin last week who's actually a detective now, and he tells me crime in the big cities is just insane compared to what it was when I was a kid.
Yeah, well, my friend who works at the precinct says it's mostly just kids running around looking for trouble, but he thinks the real problem is people who don't even live here anymore.
That's exactly what my cousin says too, about those "ghosts" in the buildings—says the owners just flipped them over to the city and now nobody cares who owns what.
Yeah, exactly. It's like they took the whole block just to let a few teenagers loose.
Yeah, that's the scary part, it's not just them hanging out, it's the stuff they get into, you know?
Yeah, it's just the little drugs and the broken windows, you know? Like nobody's fixing the porches anymore, so everyone just feels like they can take whatever they want.
Yeah, exactly. It's like if you leave a window open for five minutes, something's already gone in.

Yeah, I guess that's where my friend works too, he says it's mostly just run-down buildings waiting to happen. But you know, I have to say, that doesn't really sit right with me, because honestly, I don't think most of the people in this neighborhood are even looking for trouble. My friend says it's the absentee landlords, sure, but I think a lot of it is just... yeah, it's just that nobody's around to bother the kids anymore. Like, we used to have someone checking on us, now it's just empty rooms and broken glass. So maybe the problem isn't just the crime, but the whole place falling apart?
I see your point about the place falling apart, but my cousin says a lot of those buildings get fixed up eventually, yet the crime stays the same because of who's running the streets.

Right, so it's not the empty buildings, it's the people? Because my friend works the night shift and he says most of the guys he sees out here on the beat aren't even from the neighborhood, they're just transients looking for an easy score.
Yeah, that's what he says, the street people are different now, they're more violent, you know? Not just hanging out, actually hurting people.

Yeah, that's the part that bugs me though, I mean my friend says the drug dealers are bringing in the hard stuff, not the cheap stuff we used to see, but that just feels like it's happening way too fast.

That hard stuff part really scares me, honestly. When I was on the job back in the nineties, sure, we had kids with knives, but nobody was trying to kill your family right outside the grocery store. Now my cousin says the dealers aren't even trying to hide it anymore, they're just pushing it everywhere, and that's a whole different kind of panic.
Yeah, that's what scares me too, it feels like the whole neighborhood just turned into a marketplace for the worst stuff, and nobody's even trying to stop it like they used to.

Yeah, and it's not just the stuff they're selling, it's the way they sell it. They don't even try to look guilty anymore; my cousin says they'll walk right past a cop on the corner and just ask you for five dollars if you don't have it, and the whole family gets dragged into it before you know what's happening. It's like the line between a kid playing and a kid selling got erased completely.

Yeah, that part where they just walk up to you like it's normal? That's the worst. It's not just the drugs anymore, it's how casual they are about it. Like, my friend says he can't even tell who's a kid and who's a dealer because they're all dressed the same and acting like they own the block. It's like the whole safety net just got cut, and now everyone's just waiting for someone to try and take something from them, even if they didn't start it.
Yeah, and once you let them get that casual about it, there's no stopping it, they just keep pushing it deeper into the houses.
Yeah, once the kids get comfortable with it, you lose the whole community feeling, like everyone just shrinks back into their rooms and nobody looks out for the guy down the hall anymore.

Right, but here's the thing that's really bothering me—my cousin says it's not just the kids anymore, it's the parents just walking away from it all, like they don't even see it coming until the police show up.
Yeah, that's the worst part, I mean it feels like the adults just stepped back and let the whole thing rot until it's too late to fix.
Yeah, that's what I'm scared of, not the kids themselves, but the fact that nobody's stepping up to tell 'em no before it gets this bad.
Yeah, it's just like nobody is saying "no" anymore, so it gets harder to pull them back once they start.
Exactly, because if the adults aren't there to catch them when they slip, there's nobody left to pull the ladder down once they climb it.

Yeah, that's the thing that really gets me though, because I think the parents aren't even seeing it as a problem until it's already too late, like they're waiting for the cops to save them from themselves, and by then it's just too hard to turn it around.
Yeah, it's like they just let the kids figure it out themselves, which is why we had to involve the parents so early on.
Yeah, but I guess that's just how it goes when nobody else steps in first, like we wait for the fire department when the house is already burning down.
Yeah, and if we wait for the fire department, the house is already gone, so maybe we need to show up sooner and actually knock on the doors instead of waiting for a call.
Yeah, that's exactly it—maybe we just need to knock on more doors before the fire even starts.
Yeah, exactly, we'd have to just start knocking on every door and making sure those parents know it's about their kids before it gets out of hand.
Yeah, but knocking on every door feels like a lot of work if the people inside aren't even ready to listen, you know?
Yeah, but I guess you can't just walk up and start telling people their kids are going to jail if they don't even see it as a problem yet.
Yeah, but if they're not ready to listen, knocking on the door just makes the people inside feel attacked before you've even told them what's wrong.
Yeah, but if you don't get in there early, you can't just say "here's what you should do" because they won't even believe you.
Yeah, but if they don't even know it's a problem, who are we supposed to get in there to tell them what's wrong?
Yeah, but if you don't get in there early, nobody's gonna listen to you until it's too late, so maybe we just need to wait for the right moment before they'll even open the door.
Yeah, maybe we just need to wait for that moment, even if it feels like we're running behind the curve.
Yeah, maybe that's why I think we just gotta pick the families who are actually trying and tell 'em exactly what to do before it's too late.
Yeah, but I'm not sure waiting for them to wake up is a plan, because by the time they hear you, it's usually already gone.
Exactly, because if they don't hear it until the kids are already deep in it, we're just talking to people who are too far gone to care.
Yeah, but I guess waiting for them to realize it on their own just means we miss the window before it gets this bad.
